name: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma
aliases: inflammatory pseudotumour-like follicular dendritic cell sarcoma

clinicalPearls: A rare neoplasm arising from follicular dendritic cells, the antigen-presenting stromal cells that normally form the meshwork of lymphoid follicle germinal centres
Typically presents as a slow-growing, painless mass in cervical or other lymph nodes, or at extranodal sites such as the tonsil, abdomen, spleen or liver
Histology shows spindled to ovoid cells in whorled, storiform or fascicular patterns, characteristically admixed with small lymphocytes
The tumour cells express follicular dendritic cell markers such as CD21, CD23 and CD35, along with clusterin and podoplanin
An inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant, often in the liver or spleen, is Epstein-Barr virus associated and can mimic an inflammatory process
There is a recognised association with hyaline-vascular Castleman disease, which may precede or accompany the tumour
It behaves as a low-to-intermediate-grade sarcoma, and management is primarily complete surgical excision, with radiotherapy or chemotherapy for large, recurrent or metastatic disease
reference.pathophysiology: Follicular dendritic cell sarcoma is a mesenchymal-type neoplasm derived from the follicular dendritic cells that scaffold germinal centres and present antigen to B cells. Clonal proliferation of these stromal cells produces a spindle-cell tumour that retains its immunological markers and characteristically entraps small reactive lymphocytes. The tumour can arise de novo or in association with hyaline-vascular Castleman disease, in which dysplastic follicular dendritic meshworks may represent a precursor state. The distinctive inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant is driven by Epstein-Barr virus and shows a prominent inflammatory background. Although often indolent, the tumour can recur locally and metastasise, particularly when large, deeply sited or cytologically high-grade.
additionalDifferentials: Soft-tissue sarcoma such as gastrointestinal stromal tumour or synovial sarcoma
Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumour (for the pseudotumour-like variant)
additionalInvestigations: Excisional or core biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD21, CD23, CD35, clusterin and podoplanin
Epstein-Barr virus studies, particularly for the inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant
Cross-sectional imaging and PET-CT to define local extent and detect metastasis
Exclusion of interdigitating dendritic cell and histiocytic sarcoma by marker profile
Baseline blood tests and staging prior to treatment
redFlags: Large, rapidly enlarging or deeply sited (intra-abdominal) tumour with higher metastatic risk
Cytological high-grade features such as marked atypia, necrosis and high mitotic activity
Distant metastasis, most often to lung, liver or lymph nodes
reference.prognosis: Most tumours behave as low-to-intermediate-grade sarcomas that are curable by complete excision, but local recurrence is common and a subset metastasise; large size, deep location, high mitotic rate, necrosis and cytological atypia are associated with more aggressive behaviour and worse outcome.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the tumour as a soft-tissue sarcoma, carcinoma or inflammatory process without dendritic-cell immunostaining
Overlooking the Epstein-Barr virus-driven inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant
Failing to recognise the association with Castleman disease
Underestimating metastatic potential in large or high-grade tumours
Inadequate surgical margins leading to local recurrence
references: British and international guidance on dendritic and histiocytic neoplasms
management: Manage as a low to intermediate grade soft tissue sarcoma rather than a lymphoma, since most cases are localised and resectable at presentation
Complete surgical excision with clear margins is the primary and usually curative treatment; wide local excision is preferred over simple enucleation given the tendency for local recurrence
Consider adjuvant radiotherapy after positive or close margins, or when high risk histological features are present such as large size, deep location, high mitotic rate, or necrosis
Radiotherapy can also be used with curative or durable local control intent for unresectable but localised or locoregional disease

Reserve systemic therapy for unresectable, recurrent, high grade, or metastatic disease; there is no established standard regimen specific to this entity, so regimen choice is individualised by a sarcoma or haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team
When systemic therapy is used, it generally borrows from soft tissue sarcoma practice, including anthracycline based regimens and platinum based combinations, without dose or schedule endorsed here

For the EBV associated inflammatory pseudotumour-like variant, often hepatic or splenic and typically more indolent, favour surgical resection where feasible and reserve systemic therapy for progressive or unresectable disease
If coexisting hyaline vascular Castleman disease is identified, address it as part of the overall treatment plan since it may be a precursor or coexisting process
Targeted or biologic agents are not established as a standard line of therapy for this entity
Undertake prolonged surveillance with cross sectional imaging given the potential for late local recurrence and distant metastasis, particularly to lung and liver
Continue follow up for an extended period beyond immediate post-treatment because recurrence can occur late and behaviour is variable
Refer all suspected or confirmed cases to a specialist centre with sarcoma and haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team expertise given the rarity of the diagnosis
Refer urgently for large, rapidly enlarging, deeply sited such as intra-abdominal, or high grade appearing tumours, and for suspected or confirmed metastasis or recurrence after prior excision
